newsitem.title: UK: UK Labour woos business but nagging doubts remain.
newsitem.headline: UK Labour woos business but nagging doubts remain.

text.p: Britain's Labour Party launched its business manifesto in mid-campaign with much fanfare on Friday, but not all corporate chiefs were completely won over.

Labour leader Tony Blair unveiled his latest election push to a packed London hall. "Labor is now the party for business, the entrepreneurs champion," he said, promising low inflation, tough spending controls, no income tax rises and a cut in regulations that stifle business.

That read like a Conservative policy wish-list and Labour emphasised its pro-business credentials by parading company chiefs sympathetic to their cause, including Granada Plc chairman Gerry Robinson and Clive Hollick, head of United News & Media.

But not all business heads were won over. Tim Melville-Ross, director-general of top employers pressure group the Institute of Directors, said there were real concerns over Labour policies on the minimum wage and privatisation plans.

"The Labour Party has moved a very considerable distance over the last few years," Melville-Ross told Reuters Financial Television. "But we are going to face much greater uncertainty (under a Labour government)."
Labour enjoys a commanding lead in the polls and is poised to take power for the first time in 18 years with polling day less than three weeks away.

Its manifesto reaffirmed its commitment to introduce a minimum wage and sign the European Union's Social Chapter, which guarantees minimum employment rights. "There is no harm at all in having basic minimum standards in the workplace," Blair said. "That is in no way inconsistent with good business."

But Melville-Ross said both policies would burden business and cost jobs. "If you put them all together and add compulsory recognition of trade unions then you are talking about job losses which could be quite significant," he said.
Earlier, the ruling Conservatives, desperate to eat into Labour's yawning lead, said its plans would wreak havoc on British business.

"Just today, Labour declared themselves new friends of business," Prime Minister John Major said. "Yet he (Blair) plans to sign up to the Social Chapter, accept the Working Time Directive, hand over more trade union powers and open the gate to an unlimited stream of new regulations that the British Parliament would be unable to prevent."
The EU's Working Time Directive states that employees should not work more than 48 hours per week if they do not wish to.
Melville-Ross said Labour must also clear up its stance on privatisation. "We are still not clear on what Labour plans for privatisation and that's a problem."

The Tories have siezed on what they call a Labour U-turn on the selloff of air traffic control services. Labour says it will consider privatising the service in order to help the public finances, an apparent reversal of earlier policy.

And privatisation will have to go much further than that, Melville-Ross said. "In the long-run, selling off parts of the welfare state, such as the pension, is vital for Britain's public finances. Labour should come clean on what it plans."

With Britain's population ageing, the state pension could soon become an intolerable burden on government finances. The Conservatives have produced a long-term plan to give national insurance contributions to private sector operators to invest on people's behalf -- effectively selling off the state pension.

Robin Marshall, chief economist at Chase Manhattan, offered the financial markets' view. "Apart from the Social Chapter and minimum wage, it's difficult to find differences between Labour and the Tories. "But a year into office it may look different if they come under pressure from their own constituencies."
The markets still fear a Labour government will crumble under pressure from the trade unions -- their old paymasters -- to rectify years of public sector pay freezes.
Kevin Gardiner, Morgan Stanley's UK economist, said actions speak louder than words. "The intentions are laudable but good intentions might not be enough," he said.
